This course will center performances staged "off-stage," beyond the indoor proscenium theatre. We will examine works across multiple genres of site-specific performance, all of which interact uniquely with their locations and connect to broader interconnected social and environmental concerns. Through interaction with site, these stagings offer possibilities for rethinking the relationship between the ‘human' and ‘environmental.'

course_details.Overview of class:
What are some of the traditional forms of theatrical performances in East Asia, primarily China, Korea, and Japan? How were these traditions adapted, reworked, deconstructed, or challenged in the 20th and 21st centuries? This course first examines major traditional forms of theatre and performance in East Asia, such as Yuan drama and Beijing opera in China, mask dance drama, and pansori in Korea, and noh and bunraku in Japan. After establishing foundational knowledge in these traditional theatrical forms, the course traces how they have been adapted and shifted in relation to political, social, and cultural changes in contemporary East Asia. This course will rely on Anglophone scholarship and plays translated into English, while acknowledging that these works are only the tip of the iceberg. The course primarily centers on plays but also addresses other aesthetic embodied practices such as dance, public protests, and performance art.

course_details.Overview of class:
What can theatre and performance do in an age of the "triple planetary crisis" (climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution)? How might they help us rethink our ethical relationships with the environment, other animals, and artificial intelligence (AI)? This seminar explores how scholars and artists have grappled with these questions through theatre and performance.

We will begin by revisiting foundational critiques and debates in theatre studies that challenge the human-centered assumptions of Western theatre. While more-than-human is a capacious term, this seminar focuses on three interconnected themes: the environment, animals, and AI. Students will encounter a wide range of plays and performance forms—including realism, absurdism, and interactive performance—that engage with topics such as water pollution, the petroleum industry, the climate crisis, animal deaths, performing with/as/for animals, and the possibilities and challenges of collaborating with AI. Beyond reading and analyzing plays, we will also explore sustainable theatre practices and examine environmental activism and animal advocacy as forms of performance.

course_details.Overview of class:
How does performance respond to essential questions of society, politics and history? Theatrical practices in 20th century Germany provide ample opportunities to reflect on this question, as they unfolded in tandem with the turbulence of declining empire, revolution and world war, fascism and genocide, socialism and Cold War politics, and neoliberal economic policy. This course will explore the fantastic diversity of theatrical experimentation that has made modern Germany a hub for the emergence of new performance forms.

Together, we will consider forms such as naturalist drama, expressionism, documentary theatre and epic theatre. We will also discuss phenomena like dance theatre, cabaret and fascist spectacle, which expand the definition of performance beyond plays with spoken text. Our analysis will consider the social and political role of performance, as the artists we encounter engage with struggles around labor, gender, sexuality, race and nation. Though the primary focus is on work from the 20th century, the course also includes some contemporary pieces.

course_details.Overview of class: This class examines the role of the director in the theatre from historical, aesthetic, and practical points of view. We analyze the theatrical innovations of a variety of twentieth-century directors, including Stanislavsky, Richards, Kazan, Appia, Tairov, Meyerhold, Littlewood, Brecht, Schumann, Boal, Chong, Wolfe, Wilson, Taymor, Mnouchkine, Kaufman, and others. In each case, we consider the director in historical and artistic context, analyze their view of the theatre, and, when applicable, investigate how this view was applied in a specific production. Students engage in focused research projects on directors of their choice, experiment with production reconstruction, and approach theatre history from the perspective of performance analysis.

course_details.Overview of class:
In this advanced visual design course, students examine the expressive properties of a figure and their role in theatrical characterization. Throughout the quarter, students develop individual approaches to drawing and painting through exploration of a variety of artistic media and techniques.
Through visual research, quick gesture sketching, detailed figure drawing, and project-specific color explorations, students engage as visual storytellers, creating bold theatrical figures and cohesive characterization sets. Projects explore realistic (proportional), stylized (non-realistic), and exaggerated (fantasy) representations of the figure, as well as thematic character design through the creation of a Tarot deck or another card deck of the student's choice.

course_details.Overview of class: This course will delve into the history, context, and structure of Ancient Greek Theatre, as well as examining some of the many ways the extant texts have been interpreted and adapted through the ages. Particular focus will be brought to bear on how a variety of contexts shape the adaptation and reception of these works, and how and why these plays continue to be revived and mined for new performative opportunities even in our present day. Students will read historical and critical texts pertaining to the history, adaptation and performance of Ancient Greek Theatre, as well as reading a variety of translations/adaptations of Ancient Greek plays. This course will also include discussion, writing assignments, independent research, and in-class exercises. Final project will include a paper and presentation wherein students will propose their own adaptation of a given Ancient Greek play.

course_details.Overview of class: This course focuses on the role of the dramaturg as a creative team member helping to shape works for the musical stage, with an emphasis on new work. What makes a musical "tick? Connect with audiences? Deliver a moving, meaningful and coherent experience in the theatre? A skillful dramaturg serves as a key thought partner, researcher, and sometimes even "show doctor" collaborating with writers, composers, and directors. We will ask: How does the construction of a musical play empower, disempower, or generally position characters in relation to one another and the show's central arc? How does music effectively convey story? How is the dramaturgy of a play different from that of a musical? The reinterpretation of a classic show vs. the creation of a brand-new work? How can research into a show's history, setting and context conjure greater specificity across a musical's script and score? Students will conduct critical analysis of existing works as well as new musicals-in-progress. Guest speakers--dramaturgs from theatres in Chicago and NYC--will share insights and enhance our studies.

course_details.Overview of class: In the creation of a new musical, the composer is as much a dramatist as the lyricist or bookwriter, and the music must have dramatic integrity that is equal to and aligned with that of the show's text. In this course we will study several leading musical theatre composers who have approached the work of being a "playwright in music" in differing ways; we will then apply techniques from these artists' work to our own practice as musical theatre composers. Artists studied may include Anaïs Mitchell, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Jeanine Tesori, Jonathan Larson, Elizabeth Swados, William Finn, Stephen Flaherty, Stephen Sondheim, and Richard Rodgers. Students will analyze the musical-dramaturgical composition techniques utilized by these composers and complete music composition assignments inspired by their methods. We will workshop the submitted composition assignments together in class. This course equips students to command a range of approaches for conveying story in music, to articulate their goals as composer-dramatists in creative team meetings, and to make strong, story-driven choices in service of one's individual compositional style.

course_details.Overview of class:
Contact improvisation is a form of movement that uses physical touch and weight sharing as vehicles for spontaneous communication. In this class, we will practice rolling, falling, dynamic weight sharing, going upside down, and developing a sophisticated sense of spatial awareness. We will practice embodied and verbal communication skills around consent, and as a result, develop attention, adaptability, and resilience in our bodies. We will approach our endeavors with a sense of serious play and work to cultivate joy in our moving bodies.

We will develop skills such as mind/body integration, sensory awareness, kinesthetic empathy, and internal awareness. We will discuss and practice navigating consent in the context of a largely non-verbal social dance. We will often work in groups of two or three, dancing with classmates in a variety of situations, as well as exploring solo and ensemble improvisations. There will be weekly readings and viewings to fuel our class discussions. Previous experience with movement and/or dance is required. Please email chrissy.martin@northwestern.edu with a brief paragraph of your movement history to enroll.

No fees required, though buying a pair of dance kneepads is strongly recommended.

course_details.Overview of class: Building on the work from fall quarter and acknowledging that none of us stand alone, we will engage in experiential learning that will encourage each student to access the richness of their own cultural heritage and unique perspective to inform the personalization of their work. Specifically, uniting the voice and physical work from sophomore year, we will continue to explore and enhance our abilities to approach complicated heighten language/text, with confidence and technical acumen. This course aims to build on the foundation of the Tragedy quarter, by further examining how the use of elevated or poetic language can help the actor inhabit and communicate the needs of a character. The foundation for our understanding will be from the plays of William Shakespeare, through in-depth analysis, rehearsal and performance of a monologue and scene work. The analysis portion of the course work will include not only analysis of plot and character, but also of the elements of rhetorical form inherent in Shakespeare's writing. Student will learn to make careful and well-informed choices about their approach to character based on their analysis, but also learn to bring vitality to those choices by finding the ways in which the character connects to their own personal experience, imagination, artistry and delight in playing.

Through research, design development, interdisciplinary critique, and iterative revision, students will balance individual artistic authorship with the needs of the larger production. The course culminates in a professional-level design presentation that communicates the conceptual, visual, and practical integration of costume within the complete operatic environment.

course_details.Overview of class:
This course is about the impossible: describing the indescribable, answering questions that are unanswerable, but through that, finding ways of making synthetic connections between disparate subjects where they might not be at all apparent.

You will analyze big ideas of dramatic theory and aesthetic theory - concepts that have defined what is important about theatre and how it might be advanced as a form, and philosophical points of view concerning the beautiful, the ugly, and how we think about it. You will do this by investigating the work of thinkers within the theatre, and from the broader art-making world, from the mid 19th century to present day considering their work in their historical context and in our present circumstances.

By drawing synthetic conclusions from chronologically and philosophically incongruent sources, you will gain a more sophisticated understanding of current practice and will mature your own points of view as theatre artists. You will read curated excerpts, lead and participate in discussion, and set forth analysis and opinion in Accountability Statements and in class discussion, culminating in a Final Creative Project.

You will be exposed to a lot of dense philosophical material and asked to analyze it intellectually, and then asked to think creatively and synthetically about the material from your own perspective as an artist.

course_details.Overview of class: This course uses plays, historical context, and primary sources to examine the history of theatre in Europe, focusing on points of change and innovation, theatrical debates, and colonial legacies. How, we will ask, has this theatre responded to its own past and present? Although readings focus primarily on scripted plays and cultural context, we will investigate popular entertainment (through commedia dell' arte) and design (through analysis of chapters in undergrad textbooks), with additional self-directed research on topics ranging from individual artists to pantomime to contemporary productions. The course also includes topics likely to recur in your teaching, research, or theatrical production. The frame for the course is the frame itself. We will consider theatrical frames (the orchestra, the proscenium arch, perspective scenery, the fourth wall) and their disruptions (ironic and self-reflexive theatre, direct audience address, asides) to understand how each era positions theatre in relation to life and makes and unmakes its own rules. We will also consider how to frame theatre history for scholars, students, and theatre artists through oral presentations and a choice of final projects: syllabi, dramaturgy materials, or research papers.
